evidence.title: Informed Consent Disclosures and Minimum Requirements in AI Clinical Trials: Cross-Sectional Analysis
evidence.outcome: Consent document length and readability (SMOG) in AI trials
evidence.effect: Only 14% (n=16) of ICs met dual criteria of brevity (<15,000 characters) and readability (SMOG <13). Higher-risk trials did not show improved readability (Spearman P>.05).
evidence.quote: Only 14% (n=16) of ICs met the dual criteria of brevity (<15,000 characters) and readability (Simple Measure of Gobbledygook <13).
evidence.sample_unit: informed consent documents from AI clinical trials

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether writing AI disclosures, consent records, or privacy notices in plain language improves patient understanding. One review found that 14% of 114 AI trial consent documents met brevity and readability thresholds, while a simulation found most patients rated AI labels easy to read.

perspectives.view: No study compares plain-language disclosures with standard versions, so the practice itself has no direct evidence. The two available studies describe the hazard and point in different directions. One is a descriptive review of documents, and the other relies on self-reported comprehension in a vignette, which may overstate actual understanding.

Of 114 consent documents from AI trials, 16 (14%) were both under 15,000 characters and had a SMOG score under 13. Higher-risk trials were no more readable (P>.05). This suggests that patients in riskier AI studies may receive consent material they cannot follow. No study has tested whether shorter documents reduce misunderstanding.

A vignette study of 340 patients focused on racial and ethnic minority participants. In that study, 86.7% said the labels were easy to read and 84.2% said they were easy to understand. Self-report may miss comprehension gaps among patients with low literacy or limited English proficiency. Neither study specifically enrolled those groups or Medicaid or safety-net patients.

The CHAI playbook observes that the HIPAA Privacy Rule already requires covered entities to distribute a clear, user-friendly notice of privacy practices. The recommendation extends that expectation to AI disclosures and consent records. The supplied studies do not assess compliance. They also do not assess whether plain-language notices change what patients know or do.

Endorsing commentaries call for brief, just-in-time disclosures adapted to cognitive and digital literacy. They also ask for explicit explanations of withdrawal options and human oversight. The supplied evidence shows that lengthy consent documents are common in AI trials. It does not show that simpler versions help patients understand their rights or reach a human.

commentary.research_gap: Trials are needed that compare plain-language AI disclosures and consent forms with standard versions. Outcomes should include objective comprehension, recall of opt-out and withdrawal rights, and staff time required. These trials should enroll patients with limited English proficiency or low health literacy.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population. The one hazard study with a stated population focus enrolled racial and ethnic minority patients. Neither study included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups, so the effect of plain-language disclosures for patients most likely to struggle with technical text remains unknown.
